name: Jollof Rice
description: A rich and smoky Nigerian one-pot rice dish cooked in a flavorful tomato and pepper sauce blended with aromatic spices. Jollof Rice is one of Nigeria's most beloved meals, commonly served at parties, weddings, family gatherings, and Sunday lunches. It pairs perfectly with fried plantain, grilled chicken, turkey, beef, fish, or fresh salad.
instructions: Wash the rice thoroughly with clean water until the water runs almost clear. Drain and set aside.
Blend the fresh tomatoes, red bell peppers, Scotch bonnet peppers, one onion, garlic, and ginger into a smooth mixture.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large pot over medium heat.
Add the remaining sliced onion and sauté for about 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the tomato paste and fry for 3–5 minutes, stirring continuously to remove its raw taste.
Pour in the blended tomato mixture and cook for 15–20 minutes until the sauce thickens and the oil begins to separate from the mixture.
Add the curry powder, dried thyme, seasoning cubes, bay leaves, and salt. Stir well to combine.
Pour in the chicken stock and bring the sauce to a gentle boil.
Add the washed rice and stir until every grain is evenly coated with the sauce.
Cover the pot tightly and cook over low heat for 25–30 minutes. Add a little water or stock only if needed.
Stir gently once or twice during cooking to prevent burning without breaking the rice.
When the rice is tender and the liquid has been absorbed, remove the bay leaves, fluff the rice with a fork, and serve hot.
author: API Food Database

name: Fried Rice
description: Nigerian Fried Rice is a colorful and flavorful rice dish prepared with mixed vegetables, beef, liver, aromatic spices, and rich chicken stock. It is one of the most popular dishes served at weddings, birthdays, Christmas celebrations, and family gatherings. It is best enjoyed with fried chicken, turkey, grilled fish, or salad.
instructions: Wash the rice thoroughly and cook it in chicken stock until it is about 90% done. Drain and allow it to cool.
Season the beef with onions, seasoning cubes, thyme, curry, and salt. Cook until tender, then cut into bite-sized pieces.
Cook the chicken liver separately until tender and dice into small cubes.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large frying pan or pot over medium heat.
Add the chopped onions and sauté until fragrant.
Add the mixed vegetables, green beans, sweet corn, and green peas. Stir-fry for about 3–5 minutes.
Add the cooked beef and diced liver. Stir well.
Season with curry powder, dried thyme, white pepper, seasoning cubes, and salt.
Add the cooked rice and gently mix until every grain is coated with the vegetables and spices.
Continue stirring over low heat for about 5 minutes.
Add the chopped spring onions and stir gently.
Serve hot with fried chicken, turkey, grilled fish, moi moi, or coleslaw.
author: API Food Database

name: Egusi Soup
description: Egusi Soup is one of Nigeria's most popular traditional soups, prepared with ground melon seeds, assorted meats, smoked fish, stockfish, leafy vegetables, and rich palm oil. It is a hearty and nutritious meal enjoyed across the country and is best served with pounded yam, eba, fufu, semovita, or wheat meal.
instructions: Wash the assorted meat thoroughly and season with chopped onions, seasoning cubes, and a little salt. Cook until tender and reserve the stock.
Soak and cook the stockfish until soft. Wash the smoked fish thoroughly and remove any bones.
Mix the ground egusi with a little water until it forms a thick paste.
Heat the palm oil in a large pot over medium heat and sauté the chopped onions until fragrant.
Add the egusi paste and fry gently for about 8–10 minutes, stirring continuously until it begins to form small crumbs.
Gradually pour in the reserved meat stock while stirring until the soup reaches your preferred consistency.
Add the assorted meat, stockfish, smoked fish, crayfish, fresh pepper, locust beans, seasoning cubes, and salt.
Cover the pot and allow the soup to simmer for 15–20 minutes so all the flavors combine.
Add the chopped ugwu leaves and cook for another 3–5 minutes, just until the leaves are tender but still vibrant.
Taste and adjust the seasoning if necessary.
Serve hot with pounded yam, eba, fufu, semovita, amala, or wheat meal.
author: API Food Database

name: Nsala (White Soup)
description: Nsala, also known as White Soup, is a traditional Nigerian delicacy prepared with fresh catfish, yam paste, aromatic spices, and herbs. It is especially popular in the southeastern region of Nigeria and is commonly enjoyed with pounded yam, fufu, semovita, or eba.
instructions: Clean the catfish thoroughly using warm water and a little salt or lime juice to remove slime.
Season the fish with onions, seasoning cubes, and salt, then cook gently until almost done.
Peel and boil the yam until soft, then pound or blend it into a smooth paste.
Add the yam paste gradually into the fish stock while stirring continuously until it dissolves and thickens the soup.
Add the crayfish, fresh pepper, ground uziza seeds, and ground ehuru.
Allow the soup to simmer for about 10 minutes.
Add the sliced utazi leaves and cook for another 2–3 minutes.
Taste and adjust the seasoning if necessary.
Serve hot with pounded yam, fufu, semovita, or eba.
author: API Food Database

name: Nkwobi
description: Nkwobi is a popular Nigerian delicacy made from tender cow foot coated in a rich, spicy palm oil sauce flavored with traditional spices. It is commonly served as a delicacy in restaurants, bars, and special occasions, often enjoyed with chilled drinks.
instructions: Wash the cow foot thoroughly and place it in a pot.
Season with chopped onions, seasoning cubes, and salt, then cook until the meat becomes very soft and tender. Reserve about one cup of the stock.
Dissolve the potash in a small amount of warm water and strain to remove any particles.
Pour the palm oil into a bowl and gradually add the strained potash solution while stirring continuously until the oil becomes thick and creamy.
Add the ground crayfish, ground ehuru, blended fresh pepper, and a little of the reserved stock. Mix until smooth.
Add the cooked cow foot and stir gently until every piece is well coated with the sauce.
Add the sliced onions and chopped utazi leaves, then mix lightly.
Taste and adjust the seasoning if necessary.
Serve warm in a wooden bowl or serving dish.
author: API Food Database

name: Akara
description: Akara is a popular Nigerian bean fritter made from peeled black-eyed beans blended with onions and fresh peppers, then deep-fried until golden brown. It is commonly eaten for breakfast with pap (akamu), custard, bread, or enjoyed as a delicious snack any time of the day.
instructions: Pick through the black-eyed beans to remove stones, dirt, and damaged beans. Wash thoroughly and soak them in clean water for about 20 to 30 minutes to soften the skins.
Rub the soaked beans between your palms to loosen the skins. Rinse several times, allowing the skins to float away until most of the beans are completely peeled. Drain the peeled beans.

Transfer the peeled beans into a blender. Add the chopped onion and fresh Scotch bonnet peppers with a very small amount of water. Blend until you obtain a smooth, thick batter. Avoid adding excess water so the Akara holds its shape during frying.

Pour the batter into a large mixing bowl. Add the salt and the optional seasoning cube. Beat the mixture vigorously with a wooden spoon or whisk for about 5 minutes to incorporate air. This step helps produce soft and fluffy Akara.
Pour the vegetable oil into a deep frying pan or pot and heat over medium heat. Test the oil by dropping a little batter into it. If it rises immediately and begins to sizzle, the oil is ready.
Using a tablespoon or your hand, gently scoop portions of the batter into the hot oil. Leave enough space between each piece so they fry evenly without sticking together.
Fry for about 3 to 4 minutes on one side until golden brown. Turn each Akara carefully and fry the other side until evenly browned and fully cooked.
Remove the fried Akara with a slotted spoon and place it on paper towels or a wire rack to drain excess oil.
Serve hot with pap (akamu), custard, bread, or enjoy it on its own as a delicious Nigerian snack.

name: Pounded Yam
description: Pounded Yam is one of Nigeria's most popular swallow foods. It is made by boiling fresh yam until soft and pounding it into a smooth, stretchy dough. It is commonly served with Egusi Soup, Nsala, Ogbono Soup, Okra Soup, Vegetable Soup, and other traditional Nigerian soups.
instructions: Wash the yam thoroughly to remove any dirt. Peel off the skin with a sharp knife and rinse again with clean water.
Cut the peeled yam into medium-sized chunks of equal size so they cook evenly.
Place the yam pieces into a pot and add enough water to completely cover them.

Bring the water to a boil over medium-high heat and cook the yam for about 20–25 minutes or until it becomes very soft. Test with a fork or knife; it should pass through the yam easily without resistance.
Drain the cooked yam immediately while it is still very hot.

Transfer the hot yam into a clean mortar and pound continuously with a pestle until it becomes smooth and free of lumps. If using a food processor or yam pounding machine, process until the texture becomes soft, elastic, and stretchy.
Continue pounding, folding the dough occasionally, until the pounded yam develops a smooth, glossy appearance and can stretch slightly without breaking.

Divide into serving portions, shape into smooth balls with a little clean water if desired, and serve immediately while hot with Egusi Soup, Nsala Soup, Ogbono Soup, Okra Soup, or any soup of your choice.

name: Moi Moi
description: Moi Moi is a traditional Nigerian steamed bean pudding made from peeled black-eyed beans blended with peppers, onions, and seasonings. It is soft, nutritious, and commonly served with pap (akamu), custard, Jollof Rice, Fried Rice, garri, or enjoyed on its own as a wholesome meal.
instructions: Pick through the black-eyed beans to remove stones and damaged beans. Wash thoroughly and soak them in clean water for about 20 to 30 minutes to soften the skins.
Rub the soaked beans between your palms to remove the skins. Rinse several times until most of the skins have been removed, then drain the peeled beans.
Transfer the peeled beans into a blender. Add the chopped onion, red bell peppers (tatase), Scotch bonnet peppers, and a small amount of water. Blend until the mixture becomes very smooth and creamy.
Pour the blended batter into a large mixing bowl. Add the palm oil, crayfish, seasoning cubes, and salt. Stir thoroughly until all the ingredients are evenly combined.
Lightly grease Moi Moi containers, ramekins, or banana leaves with a little palm oil. Pour the batter into each container, filling them about three-quarters full to allow room for expansion.
If using boiled eggs or other fillings such as smoked fish, corned beef, or shrimp, place them gently into the center of each filled container before steaming.

Arrange the containers in a large pot. Pour hot water into the pot until it reaches about one-third of the height of the containers. Cover the containers with foil if necessary and close the pot tightly with a lid.
Steam over medium heat for about 45 to 50 minutes. Check the water level occasionally and add more hot water whenever necessary to prevent the pot from drying out.
Insert a toothpick or knife into the center of one Moi Moi. If it comes out clean, the Moi Moi is fully cooked.
Carefully remove the containers from the pot and allow them to cool slightly before serving. Serve hot with pap (akamu), custard, Jollof Rice, Fried Rice, garri, or enjoy it on its own.

name: Suya
description: Suya is one of Nigeria's most famous street foods, made by coating thin slices of beef in spicy yaji (suya spice), skewering them, and grilling until smoky and tender. It is traditionally served with sliced onions, tomatoes, cabbage, and an extra sprinkle of yaji for a bold, flavorful experience.
instructions: If using wooden skewers, soak them in clean water for about 20 minutes to prevent them from burning during grilling.
Wash the beef thoroughly and slice it into very thin strips, about ¼ cm thick. Thin slices absorb the suya spice better and cook more evenly.

Place the beef in a large bowl. Add the seasoning cube, salt, half of the suya spice, and one tablespoon of vegetable oil. Mix thoroughly until every piece of beef is evenly coated. Cover and allow it to marinate for at least 20 minutes. For a richer flavor, marinate for up to 2 hours in the refrigerator.
Thread the marinated beef slices onto the soaked skewers, folding the meat as necessary to keep it firmly in place.
Brush the skewered beef lightly with the remaining vegetable oil, then sprinkle the remaining suya spice generously over both sides.
Preheat a charcoal grill, barbecue grill, grill pan, or oven grill over medium-high heat.
Grill the skewers for about 5 to 7 minutes on each side, turning occasionally until the beef is browned, slightly charred around the edges, and fully cooked.
Remove the Suya from the grill and sprinkle a little extra yaji over the hot meat if you enjoy a spicier flavor.
Slice the onions, tomatoes, and cabbage into thin strips and arrange them on a serving plate.
Serve the hot Suya immediately with the sliced vegetables and extra yaji on the side.
author: API Food Database

name: Goat Meat Pepper Soup
description: Goat Meat Pepper Soup is a classic Nigerian delicacy prepared with tender goat meat simmered in a flavorful broth made with traditional pepper soup spices, fresh peppers, and aromatic herbs. It is commonly enjoyed as an appetizer, a light meal, or alongside chilled drinks.
instructions: Wash the goat meat thoroughly and place it in a large pot.
Add the chopped onions, seasoning cubes, salt, and about one cup of water. Cover the pot and cook over medium heat until the goat meat begins to release its natural juices.
Pour in the remaining water and continue cooking for about 35 to 40 minutes, or until the meat becomes tender. Add more water if necessary to maintain a rich broth.
Blend or crush the fresh peppers and add them to the pot together with the pepper soup spice. Stir well to combine.
Allow the soup to simmer for another 10 minutes so the spices fully infuse the broth.
Wash and slice the utazi leaves into thin strips. Add them to the soup and cook for another 2 to 3 minutes. Avoid overcooking so they retain their characteristic flavor.
Taste the broth and adjust the seasoning with additional salt if necessary.
Remove the pot from the heat and serve the Goat Meat Pepper Soup hot. It can be enjoyed on its own or with boiled yam, boiled plantain, or white rice.

name: Ofe Onugbu (Bitter Leaf Soup)
description: Ofe Onugbu, popularly known as Bitter Leaf Soup, is a rich traditional Igbo soup prepared with washed bitter leaves, cocoyam paste, assorted meats, stockfish, smoked fish, palm oil, and aromatic seasonings. Despite its name, properly washed bitter leaves give the soup a pleasant earthy flavor that pairs perfectly with pounded yam, fufu, eba, or semovita.
instructions: Wash the assorted meat thoroughly and place it in a large cooking pot. Add the seasoning cubes, a little salt, and enough water to cover the meat. Cook over medium heat until the meat becomes tender.
Wash the stockfish thoroughly and add it to the pot. Continue cooking until it softens. Add the smoked fish carefully, ensuring any bones or dirt have been removed.
Peel the cocoyam and boil it separately until it becomes soft. Pound or blend it into a smooth paste and set it aside.

Wash the bitter leaves thoroughly if using fresh leaves. Rinse several times until the bitterness is reduced but not completely removed. If using already washed bitter leaves, rinse once before cooking.
Blend or crush the fresh pepper and add it to the meat stock. Stir in the crayfish and allow the soup to boil for about 5 minutes so the flavors begin to develop.
Pour in the palm oil and allow it to cook for another 5 minutes.
Add the cocoyam paste in small portions while stirring gently. Allow it to dissolve completely into the soup. Continue cooking until the soup thickens to your desired consistency.
Add the washed bitter leaves and stir well to combine. Cook for another 8 to 10 minutes so the leaves soften while still retaining their flavor.
Taste the soup and adjust the seasoning with additional salt if necessary. Allow it to simmer for another 2 to 3 minutes.
Remove the soup from the heat and serve hot with pounded yam, fufu, eba, semovita, or any swallow of your choice.
author: API Food Database

name: Banga Soup
description: Banga Soup is a rich and aromatic delicacy native to the Niger Delta region of Nigeria. It is prepared from fresh palm fruit extract, catfish, traditional Banga spices, crayfish, and fresh scent leaves. The soup is best enjoyed with starch, pounded yam, fufu, or eba.
instructions: Wash the fresh palm fruits thoroughly and place them in a large pot. Add enough water to cover them and boil for about 30 to 40 minutes until they become soft.
Drain the cooked palm fruits into a mortar and pound gently to loosen the pulp from the nuts. Alternatively, mash them with a sturdy spoon.
Add warm water to the mashed palm fruits and squeeze thoroughly with your hands to extract the thick palm fruit juice. Strain the extract into a clean pot, leaving the nuts and fibres behind.
Bring the palm fruit extract to a boil over medium heat and cook for about 15 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally until the liquid begins to thicken and the natural palm oil rises to the surface.
While the extract is cooking, clean the catfish carefully using warm water and a little salt or lime juice to remove the slime. Cut it into serving pieces if necessary.
Blend or crush the fresh pepper and add it to the boiling palm fruit extract together with the chopped onions, ground crayfish, Banga spice, seasoning cubes, and salt. Stir well to combine.
Carefully add the catfish into the soup and cook gently for about 10 to 12 minutes. Avoid excessive stirring to prevent the fish from breaking apart.
Wash and slice the scent leaves, then stir them into the soup. Allow the soup to simmer for another 2 to 3 minutes so the aroma of the leaves develops fully.
Taste the soup and adjust the seasoning if necessary. Remove from the heat once the soup is rich, fragrant, and slightly thickened.
Serve hot with starch, pounded yam, fufu, semovita, or eba.
author: API Food Database

name: Ogbono Soup
description: Ogbono Soup is a rich and nutritious Nigerian soup made from ground wild mango (ogbono) seeds, known for its distinctive slippery texture. It is cooked with palm oil, assorted proteins, crayfish, and leafy vegetables, making it a delicious meal best enjoyed with eba, pounded yam, fufu, semovita, or other swallows.
instructions: Wash the beef thoroughly and place it in a large cooking pot. Add the seasoning cubes, a little salt, and enough water to cover the meat. Cook over medium heat until the beef becomes tender.
Wash the stockfish thoroughly and add it to the pot. Continue cooking until it softens. Add the smoked fish after removing any dirt or loose bones.
Blend or pound the fresh pepper and add it to the pot together with the crayfish. Allow the stock to boil for about 5 minutes so the flavors combine.
Pour the palm oil into a clean bowl and add the ground ogbono seeds. Mix thoroughly until you have a smooth paste without lumps.
Gradually stir the ogbono mixture into the boiling meat stock while stirring continuously. This helps the soup develop its characteristic smooth and stretchy texture.
Reduce the heat and allow the soup to cook for about 10 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent the ogbono from sticking to the bottom of the pot.
Wash the ugwu leaves thoroughly and slice them into thin strips. Add them to the soup and stir gently.
Allow the soup to cook for another 3 to 5 minutes. Avoid overcooking the vegetables so they remain fresh and vibrant.
Taste the soup and adjust the seasoning with additional salt if necessary. If the soup becomes too thick, add a little hot water until you achieve your preferred consistency.
Remove the soup from the heat and serve hot with eba, pounded yam, fufu, semovita, or any swallow of your choice.
author: API Food Database

name: Efo Riro
description: Efo Riro is a popular Yoruba vegetable soup prepared with fresh spinach or ugwu leaves, assorted meats, smoked fish, palm oil, and a rich pepper sauce. It is nutritious, flavorful, and commonly enjoyed with pounded yam, amala, eba, fufu, or rice.
instructions: Wash the assorted meat thoroughly and place it in a large pot. Add the seasoning cubes, a little salt, and enough water to cover the meat. Cook until the meat becomes tender. Add the smoked fish during the last few minutes of cooking after cleaning it properly.
Wash the spinach or ugwu leaves thoroughly. Slice them into thin strips and set aside.
Blend the tatashe, tomatoes, Scotch bonnet peppers, and one onion until smooth. If you prefer a slightly textured soup, pulse the blender instead of blending completely.
Heat the palm oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the remaining chopped onion and fry for about 2 minutes until fragrant.
Pour the blended pepper mixture into the hot oil and fry for about 15 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens and the palm oil begins to separate from the pepper mixture.
Add the cooked assorted meat together with some of the meat stock into the pepper sauce. Stir in the crayfish and cook for another 5 minutes so the flavors combine.
Taste the soup and adjust with additional seasoning cubes or salt if necessary.
Add the sliced spinach or ugwu leaves and stir gently until the vegetables are evenly distributed throughout the soup.
Cook for another 3 to 5 minutes. Do not overcook the vegetables so they remain fresh, green, and nutritious.
Remove the soup from the heat and serve hot with amala, pounded yam, eba, fufu, semovita, or even white rice.
author: API Food Database

name: Afang Soup
description: Afang Soup is a rich and nutritious delicacy native to the Efik and Ibibio people of Cross River and Akwa Ibom States. It is prepared with finely sliced afang (okazi) leaves, tender waterleaf, assorted meats, seafood, palm oil, and traditional seasonings. This flavorful soup is best enjoyed with pounded yam, eba, fufu, semovita, or other Nigerian swallows.
instructions: Wash the assorted meat thoroughly and place it in a large pot. Add the seasoning cubes, a little salt, and enough water to cover the meat. Cook over medium heat until the meat becomes tender.
Wash the stockfish thoroughly and add it to the pot. Continue cooking until it softens. Clean the smoked fish carefully to remove dirt and loose bones, then add it to the pot.
Wash the periwinkle thoroughly if using fresh periwinkle to remove sand and dirt. Set it aside.
Wash the waterleaf thoroughly and chop it into smaller pieces if the leaves are large. Wash the sliced afang leaves separately and set them aside.
Blend or crush the fresh pepper and add it to the meat stock together with the crayfish. Stir well and allow the soup to boil for about 5 minutes so the flavors combine.
Pour in the palm oil and stir thoroughly. Allow the soup to cook for another 5 minutes until the oil blends well with the stock.
Add the waterleaf and cook for about 5 minutes. The waterleaf will release its natural moisture, enriching the soup.
Stir in the sliced afang leaves and mix thoroughly until they are evenly distributed throughout the soup.
Add the cleaned periwinkle and continue cooking for another 8 to 10 minutes, allowing all the ingredients to blend together.
Taste the soup and adjust the seasoning with additional salt if necessary. If the soup is too thick, add a little hot water until you reach your preferred consistency.
Remove the soup from the heat and serve hot with pounded yam, eba, fufu, semovita, or any Nigerian swallow of your choice.
author: API Food Database

name: Edikang Ikong
description: Edikang Ikong is a luxurious vegetable soup native to the Efik and Ibibio people of Cross River and Akwa Ibom States. It is prepared with generous amounts of fluted pumpkin (ugwu) leaves, waterleaf, assorted meats, seafood, palm oil, and traditional seasonings. Rich in nutrients and flavor, it is best served with pounded yam, starch, eba, fufu, or semovita.
instructions: Wash the assorted meat thoroughly and place it in a large cooking pot. Add the seasoning cubes, a little salt, and enough water to cover the meat. Cook over medium heat until the meat becomes tender.

Wash the stockfish thoroughly and add it to the pot. Continue cooking until it softens. Clean the smoked fish to remove dirt and loose bones, then add it to the pot during the last few minutes of cooking.
Wash the periwinkle thoroughly several times to remove sand and dirt. Set it aside.
Wash the ugwu leaves and waterleaf separately. Slice the ugwu leaves into thin strips if they are not already sliced. Chop the waterleaf into smaller pieces if necessary.
Blend or crush the fresh pepper and add it to the meat stock together with the crayfish. Stir well and allow the soup to boil for about 5 minutes.
Pour in the palm oil and stir thoroughly until it combines with the stock.
Add the chopped waterleaf first and cook for about 5 minutes. The waterleaf will release its natural moisture and help create the rich texture of the soup.
Add the ugwu leaves and stir gently until they are evenly distributed throughout the soup.
Add the cleaned periwinkle and continue cooking for another 5 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Taste the soup and adjust the seasoning with additional salt if necessary. If the soup becomes too thick, add a small amount of hot water until you achieve your preferred consistency.
Remove the soup from the heat and serve hot with pounded yam, starch, eba, fufu, semovita, or any Nigerian swallow of your choice.
author: API Food Database

name: Oha Soup
description: Oha Soup is a cherished traditional Igbo delicacy prepared with tender fresh oha leaves, cocoyam as a natural thickener, palm oil, assorted meats, stockfish, smoked fish, and aromatic seasonings. The soft, delicate texture of the oha leaves gives the soup its unique taste, making it a favorite accompaniment for pounded yam, fufu, eba, or semovita.
instructions: Wash the assorted meat thoroughly and place it in a large cooking pot. Add the seasoning cubes, a little salt, and enough water to cover the meat. Cook over medium heat until the meat becomes tender.
Wash the stockfish thoroughly and add it to the pot. Continue cooking until it softens. Clean the smoked fish carefully to remove dirt and loose bones before adding it to the pot.
Peel the cocoyam, wash it thoroughly, and boil it separately until soft. Pound or blend it into a smooth paste and set it aside.

Wash the fresh Oha leaves carefully. Remove the leaves gently from the stalks using your hands instead of cutting them with a knife, as this helps preserve their delicate texture. Rinse and set aside.
Blend or crush the fresh pepper and add it to the meat stock together with the crayfish. Allow the soup to boil for about 5 minutes so the flavors combine.
Pour the palm oil into the soup and stir thoroughly. Allow it to cook for another 5 minutes until the oil blends well with the stock.
Add the cocoyam paste in small portions while stirring gently until it dissolves completely. Continue cooking until the soup thickens naturally.
Taste the soup and adjust the seasoning with additional salt if necessary. If the soup becomes too thick, add a little hot water until you reach your desired consistency.
Add the fresh Oha leaves and stir gently. Cook for only 2 to 3 minutes, as Oha leaves lose their flavor and texture if overcooked.
Remove the soup from the heat immediately and serve hot with pounded yam, fufu, eba, semovita, or any Nigerian swallow of your choice.
author: API Food Database

name: Ofada Stew (Ayamase)
description: Ofada Stew, popularly known as Ayamase, is a rich and spicy Yoruba delicacy prepared with green and red tatashe, scotch bonnet peppers, fermented locust beans (iru), bleached palm oil, and assorted meats. It is famous for its bold aroma, smoky flavor, and is traditionally served with Ofada rice, although it also pairs well with plain white rice.
instructions: Wash the assorted meat thoroughly and place it in a large pot. Add the seasoning cubes, a little salt, chopped onions, and enough water to cover the meat. Cook over medium heat until the meat becomes tender. Reserve the meat stock.
Wash the green and red tatashe together with the Scotch bonnet peppers. Remove the seeds if you prefer a milder stew, then blend the peppers coarsely without adding too much water.

Pour the palm oil into a clean pot and carefully bleach it over medium heat. Allow the oil to heat until it changes from bright red to a darker golden-brown color and light smoke begins to appear. Turn off the heat and allow the oil to cool slightly before continuing. This step gives authentic Ofada stew its distinctive smoky flavor.
Return the pot to low heat and add the chopped onions. Fry for about 2 minutes until they soften.
Add the iru (locust beans) and stir continuously for another 2 to 3 minutes to release its rich aroma.

Pour the blended pepper mixture into the bleached palm oil and stir thoroughly. Cook uncovered over medium heat for about 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until most of the moisture evaporates and the palm oil begins to separate and float on top.
Add the cooked assorted meat together with a small amount of the reserved meat stock. Stir well so the meat absorbs the rich pepper mixture.

Taste the stew and adjust the seasoning with additional seasoning cubes or salt if necessary. Continue cooking for another 10 to 15 minutes until the stew becomes thick and the oil floats clearly on the surface.
Remove the stew from the heat and allow it to rest for about 5 minutes before serving.
Serve hot with authentic Ofada rice, white rice, boiled yam, or boiled plantain.
author: API Food Database

name: Abacha (African Salad)
description: Abacha, popularly known as African Salad, is a beloved Igbo delicacy prepared from shredded dried cassava, palm oil, ugba (African oil bean), crayfish, garden eggs, smoked fish, and traditional seasonings. It is a refreshing, flavorful dish enjoyed as a light meal, snack, or appetizer throughout Eastern Nigeria.
instructions: Place the dried abacha in a large bowl and pour warm water over it. Allow it to soak for about 10 to 15 minutes until it becomes soft but not mushy. Drain thoroughly and set aside.
Dissolve the potash in about two tablespoons of warm water. Strain the solution to remove any particles.
Pour the palm oil into a clean mixing bowl. Gradually add the strained potash solution while stirring continuously until the palm oil changes to a bright yellow, creamy mixture.
Add the ground crayfish, ground calabash nutmeg (ehuru), seasoning cubes, salt, and blended fresh pepper to the palm oil mixture. Mix thoroughly until well combined.
Add the soaked abacha into the seasoned palm oil mixture and toss gently until every strand is evenly coated.
Wash the ugba thoroughly and add it to the mixture. Stir gently to combine.
Clean the smoked fish, remove the bones, flake it into smaller pieces, and mix it into the salad.
Wash and slice the garden eggs into bite-sized pieces. Add them to the bowl and mix gently without crushing them.
Taste the salad and adjust the seasoning if necessary. Allow it to rest for about 5 minutes so the flavors blend together.
Serve immediately at room temperature. Garnish with extra garden eggs, onions, or utazi leaves if desired.
author: API Food Database

name: Gbegiri Soup
description: Gbegiri Soup is a smooth and creamy Yoruba bean soup prepared from peeled brown beans, onions, crayfish, palm oil, and traditional seasonings. It is famous for its silky texture and is traditionally served with ewedu, Ofada stew, and amala to create the classic Yoruba meal known as Abula.
instructions: Pick through the brown beans to remove stones and dirt. Wash them thoroughly in clean water.

Soak the beans in warm water for about 30 minutes or longer if desired. Rub the beans gently between your palms to loosen the skins, then rinse repeatedly until most of the skins are removed. Drain away the skins.

Place the peeled beans in a cooking pot with the chopped onions and enough water to cover them completely. Cook over medium heat until the beans become very soft. Add more water during cooking if necessary.
Blend or mash the cooked beans until completely smooth. For a traditional silky texture, pass the blended beans through a sieve to remove any remaining bean skins.
Return the smooth bean puree to the pot and place it over low heat. Stir continuously to prevent it from sticking to the bottom.
Add the palm oil, ground crayfish, blended fresh pepper, seasoning cubes, and salt. Stir thoroughly until everything is well combined.
Allow the soup to simmer gently for about 10 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally until it becomes smooth, creamy, and slightly thick.
Taste the soup and adjust the seasoning if necessary. If it becomes too thick, add a little hot water until you achieve your preferred consistency.
Remove the soup from the heat once it reaches a silky texture.
Serve hot with amala, alongside ewedu soup and Ofada stew to enjoy the classic Yoruba Abula meal. It can also be served with eba or other Nigerian swallows.

name: Chicken Stir Fry
description: Chicken Stir Fry is a colorful continental dish made with tender chicken breast, crisp vegetables, garlic, ginger, and a savory soy sauce. Cooked quickly over high heat, it delivers fresh flavors, plenty of protein, and a satisfying crunch. It is perfect for serving with steamed rice, fried rice, noodles, or mashed potatoes.

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (carrots, green beans, bell peppers)

Season the chicken with one seasoning cube, half of the soy sauce, and half of the black pepper. Mix well and allow it to marinate for about 15 minutes while you prepare the vegetables.

Wash all the vegetables thoroughly. Slice the carrots into thin strips, trim the green beans, cut the bell peppers into strips, slice the onion thinly, finely chop the garlic, and grate the fresh ginger.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large wok or frying pan over high heat until it becomes hot.
Add the chopped garlic and grated ginger to the hot oil and stir continuously for about 30 seconds until fragrant. Be careful not to let them burn.
Add the sliced onions and stir-fry for about one minute until they begin to soften.
Add the marinated chicken strips and cook over high heat for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring frequently, until the chicken is fully cooked and lightly browned.
Add the carrots and green beans first since they require a slightly longer cooking time. Stir-fry for about 2 minutes before adding the bell peppers and any other soft vegetables.

Pour in the remaining soy sauce, add the remaining seasoning cube, and sprinkle in the remaining black pepper. Toss everything together continuously so the sauce coats both the chicken and vegetables evenly.
Continue cooking for another 2 to 3 minutes until the vegetables are tender but still crisp. Avoid overcooking to preserve their color, texture, and nutrients.
Taste the stir fry and adjust the seasoning if necessary. Remove from the heat immediately once everything is well combined.
Serve hot with steamed rice, fried rice, noodles, mashed potatoes, or enjoy it on its own as a healthy, protein-rich meal.

name: Grilled Chicken and Chips
description: Grilled Chicken and Chips is a classic continental meal featuring juicy, well-marinated chicken grilled until perfectly charred and served with crispy golden potato chips. This satisfying dish is ideal for family dinners, weekend treats, or special occasions and pairs wonderfully with coleslaw or a fresh vegetable salad.
instructions: Wash the chicken thoroughly and pat it dry with paper towels. If using a whole chicken, cut it into serving portions.

Blend or finely grate the onion and garlic. In a large bowl, combine the onion, garlic, mixed spice, paprika, black pepper, soy sauce, seasoning cubes, salt, and one tablespoon of vegetable oil to make a rich marinade.
Rub the marinade generously over every piece of chicken, ensuring it is well coated. Cover and refrigerate or leave to marinate for at least 30 minutes. For deeper flavor, marinate for 2 to 4 hours.

Preheat your oven or grill to 180°C. Arrange the chicken pieces on a baking tray or grill rack. Grill or bake for 35 to 45 minutes, turning halfway through and brushing with the pan juices or a little oil until the chicken is fully cooked with a golden-brown exterior.
While the chicken is cooking, peel the potatoes and cut them into evenly sized strips. Rinse them in cold water to remove excess starch, then pat them completely dry with a clean towel.
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the potato strips in batches for 5 to 6 minutes until lightly cooked. Remove and allow them to rest for about 5 minutes.
Increase the heat slightly and fry the potatoes a second time for 2 to 3 minutes until they become crispy and golden brown. Remove them and drain on paper towels.
Lightly sprinkle the hot chips with a little salt and toss gently.
Arrange the grilled chicken alongside the crispy chips on a serving plate. Serve immediately with coleslaw, ketchup, chili sauce, garlic sauce, or a fresh garden salad.

name: Vegetable Omelette
description: Vegetable Omelette is a quick, fluffy, and nutritious breakfast made with fresh eggs, onions, tomatoes, bell peppers, carrots, and simple seasonings. Packed with protein and colorful vegetables, it is perfect for breakfast, brunch, or a light dinner and pairs well with bread, toast, fried plantain, or potatoes.
instructions: Crack the eggs into a large mixing bowl. Add the crushed seasoning cubes, black pepper, and salt, then whisk thoroughly until the eggs become light, smooth, and slightly frothy.
Wash the onion, tomato, green bell pepper, and carrot thoroughly. Finely chop the onion, tomato, and bell pepper, then grate or finely dice the carrot so it cooks quickly.
Add all the chopped vegetables to the beaten eggs and stir until they are evenly distributed throughout the mixture.
Heat the vegetable oil in a non-stick frying pan over medium heat until it is hot but not smoking.
Pour the egg mixture into the pan and gently spread it evenly using a spatula. Reduce the heat to low to allow the eggs to cook evenly without burning.
Cook undisturbed for about 3 to 4 minutes until the bottom is golden brown and the top begins to set.
Using a spatula, carefully fold the omelette in half or flip it over if you prefer. Cook for another 2 to 3 minutes until the eggs are fully cooked while remaining soft and fluffy.
Transfer the omelette to a serving plate and allow it to rest for about one minute before serving.
Serve hot with toasted bread, buttered toast, fried potatoes, fried plantain, baked beans, sausages, or a fresh vegetable salad.

name: Coleslaw
description: A creamy and crunchy Nigerian-style coleslaw made with shredded cabbage, carrots, and a sweet mayonnaise dressing. A popular side dish at parties and gatherings.
instructions: Shred cabbage thinly with a knife or grater.
Grate or julienne carrots.
Mix mayonnaise, sugar, and salt in a bowl.
Toss cabbage and carrots in the dressing.
Refrigerate for 30 minutes before serving.
Serve as a side dish.

name: Coleslaw
description: Coleslaw is a creamy and refreshing salad made with finely shredded cabbage, carrots, and a rich mayonnaise dressing. Popular at Nigerian parties, restaurants, and family gatherings, it pairs perfectly with fried rice, jollof rice, grilled chicken, barbecue, and other continental meals.
instructions: Remove the tough outer leaves of the cabbage and wash it thoroughly under running water. Slice it into very thin strips using a sharp knife or shred it with a grater.
Wash and peel the carrots, then grate them using the large holes of a grater or cut them into thin julienne strips.
Transfer the shredded cabbage and grated carrots into a large mixing bowl and toss them together until evenly combined.
In a separate bowl, combine the mayonnaise, evaporated milk (if using), sugar, and salt. Stir well until the dressing becomes smooth and creamy.
Pour the dressing over the vegetables and mix thoroughly using a spoon or salad tongs until every strand of cabbage and carrot is evenly coated.
Taste the coleslaw and adjust the seasoning if necessary by adding a little more mayonnaise or salt according to your preference.
Cover the bowl with plastic wrap or a lid and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes. Chilling allows the flavors to blend together and gives the salad a crisp, refreshing texture.
Stir the coleslaw once more before serving. Serve chilled alongside fried rice, jollof rice, grilled chicken, barbecue, fried chicken, burgers, sandwiches, or other continental dishes.

name: Pancakes
description: Pancakes are soft, fluffy, and lightly golden breakfast treats made from flour, eggs, milk, and simple baking ingredients. They are quick to prepare and can be served with honey, maple syrup, chocolate spread, fresh fruits, or condensed milk for a delicious breakfast or brunch.
instructions: In a large mixing bowl, combine the all-purpose flour, baking powder, sugar, and salt. Mix thoroughly so the dry ingredients are evenly distributed.
In another bowl, crack the eggs and whisk until smooth. Add the milk, melted butter, and vanilla essence, then whisk again until everything is well combined.
Gradually pour the wet mixture into the bowl of dry ingredients while whisking continuously. Mix until you have a smooth batter with little or no lumps. Avoid overmixing to keep the pancakes soft.
Allow the batter to rest for about 5 to 10 minutes. This helps the flour absorb the liquid and results in fluffier pancakes.
Place a non-stick frying pan over medium heat and lightly grease it with the vegetable oil or a little butter.
Pour about a quarter cup of batter into the hot pan and allow it to spread naturally into a round shape.
Cook for about 2 to 3 minutes, or until bubbles begin to appear on the surface and the edges start to dry.
Carefully flip the pancake using a spatula and cook the other side for another 1 to 2 minutes until golden brown.
Repeat the process with the remaining batter, lightly greasing the pan before each new batch if necessary.
Serve the pancakes warm with honey, maple syrup, chocolate spread, jam, condensed milk, fresh fruits, or your favorite topping.

name: Chicken Shawarma
description: Chicken Shawarma is one of Nigeria's most popular street foods. It features juicy, well-seasoned chicken strips wrapped in soft shawarma bread with creamy garlic sauce, crunchy coleslaw, fresh vegetables, and toasted until lightly crispy. It is perfect as a quick lunch, dinner, or satisfying snack.
instructions: Wash the chicken breast thoroughly and cut it into thin strips. Pat it dry with a paper towel before seasoning.
In a bowl, combine the chicken with the shawarma spice and a little salt if desired. Mix well until every piece is evenly coated, then leave it to marinate for 20 to 30 minutes.

Heat the vegetable oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the marinated chicken strips and cook for about 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is fully cooked, juicy, and lightly browned.
Wash the tomato and onion thoroughly. Slice them into thin rings or strips and set them aside.
Warm each shawarma bread in a dry frying pan for about 20 to 30 seconds on each side until it becomes soft and flexible without becoming crispy.
Spread one tablespoon of garlic sauce evenly over each shawarma bread. Add a layer of coleslaw, followed by the cooked chicken, sliced onions, and tomatoes.
Fold the left and right edges of the bread inward, then roll it tightly from the bottom upward to keep the filling secure inside.
Place the wrapped shawarma back into the frying pan or a sandwich press and toast for about 2 to 3 minutes on each side until the outside becomes golden brown and slightly crispy.
Remove from the heat, cut each shawarma into halves if preferred, and serve immediately while hot with fries, a chilled drink, or extra garlic sauce.
author: API Food Database

name: Spaghetti Bolognese
description: Spaghetti Bolognese is a hearty pasta dish made with tender spaghetti coated in a rich tomato and minced beef sauce. Flavored with onions, garlic, herbs, and spices, this Italian-inspired meal has become a family favorite in many Nigerian homes because it is filling, delicious, and easy to prepare.
instructions: Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Add a teaspoon of salt, then add the spaghetti and cook according to the package instructions until it is tender but still firm (al dente). Drain the water and set the spaghetti aside. You may drizzle a little vegetable oil over it to prevent it from sticking together.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large frying pan or saucepan over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and minced garlic, then sauté for about 2 to 3 minutes until they become soft and fragrant.
Add the minced beef to the pan and use a wooden spoon to break it into small pieces. Cook for about 8 to 10 minutes until the beef is browned and no pink parts remain.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for another 2 to 3 minutes while stirring continuously. This removes the raw taste of the tomato paste and enhances the flavor.
Add the mixed herbs, black pepper, seasoning cubes, and salt. Pour in about half a cup of water and stir until everything is well combined.
Reduce the heat to low and allow the sauce to simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally until it becomes rich, thick, and flavorful.
Add the cooked spaghetti to the sauce and gently toss until every strand is evenly coated with the meat sauce. Alternatively, serve the sauce on top of the spaghetti if preferred.
Taste the dish and adjust the seasoning if necessary. Serve hot with garlic bread, grilled chicken, fresh salad, or grated Parmesan cheese if available.

name: Vegetable Fried Rice
description: Vegetable Fried Rice is a light, colorful, and nutritious one-pan meal made with fluffy rice, scrambled eggs, crunchy mixed vegetables, and a savory soy sauce seasoning. It is quick to prepare, budget-friendly, and perfect for lunch or dinner.

instructions: Cook the rice ahead of time until it is just tender. Spread it on a tray or large plate and allow it to cool completely. Cold rice works best because the grains remain separate during frying.
Crack the eggs into a bowl, add a pinch of salt, and whisk until well combined.
Heat half of the vegetable oil in a large frying pan or wok over medium-high heat. Pour in the eggs and gently scramble until just cooked. Remove the eggs from the pan and set them aside.
Add the remaining vegetable oil to the same pan. Add the chopped onion and garlic, then sauté for about 2 minutes until fragrant and slightly softened.
Add the mixed vegetables and stir-fry for 3 to 5 minutes until they become tender but still retain a slight crunch.
Add the cooked rice to the pan and gently stir everything together so the vegetables are evenly distributed throughout the rice.
Pour in the soy sauce, then add the black pepper and salt. Continue stirring for another 3 to 5 minutes so the rice absorbs all the flavors and heats through evenly.
Return the scrambled eggs to the pan and gently fold them into the rice. Stir for about one minute until everything is well combined.
Taste the fried rice and adjust the seasoning if necessary. Serve hot on its own or with grilled chicken, stir-fried beef, fish, or any protein of your choice.

name: Ewa Agoyin
description: Ewa Agoyin is a famous Lagos street food made with very soft honey beans served with a rich, smoky, spicy pepper sauce prepared with palm oil, onions, and dry pepper. It is traditionally paired with freshly baked Agege bread for a hearty and satisfying meal enjoyed at breakfast, lunch, or dinner.
instructions: Pick through the honey beans to remove stones and dirt, then rinse thoroughly under clean running water. Transfer the beans into a large pot, add enough water to cover them completely, and cook over medium heat for about 50 to 60 minutes until the beans become very soft. Add more water whenever necessary to prevent the beans from drying out.

When the beans are fully cooked, add the seasoning cubes and salt. Using a wooden spoon or potato masher, mash the beans until smooth, leaving a few whole beans if you prefer a little texture. Keep the mashed beans warm while you prepare the sauce.

Peel and thinly slice the onions. Pour the palm oil into a saucepan and heat it over medium heat until it becomes hot. Add the sliced onions and fry them slowly until they become very dark brown and caramelized. Stir frequently to avoid burning them completely.

Add the dry pepper to the caramelized onions and stir continuously. Fry the mixture for another 8 to 10 minutes until the pepper loses its raw taste and the oil develops a rich, smoky aroma. This pepper sauce is what gives authentic Ewa Agoyin its distinctive flavor.
Taste the sauce and adjust the seasoning if needed. The sauce should be rich, spicy, slightly smoky, and generously coated with palm oil.
Scoop the warm mashed beans into serving bowls or plates and generously spoon the pepper sauce over the top.
Slice the Agege bread and serve alongside the beans while everything is still hot. Ewa Agoyin is best enjoyed fresh with cold water, soft drinks, or pap.

name: Nigerian Tomato Stew with Chicken
description: Nigerian Tomato Stew with Chicken is a rich, flavorful stew made with fresh tomatoes, tatashe, onions, and well-seasoned chicken simmered in vegetable oil. It is one of the most popular Nigerian stews and pairs perfectly with white rice, boiled yam, plantain, bread, potatoes, or pasta.
instructions: Wash the chicken thoroughly and place it in a pot. Add the chopped onion, seasoning cubes, curry powder, thyme, salt, and a little water. Cook over medium heat for about 20 minutes or until the chicken becomes tender. Reserve the chicken stock.
Remove the cooked chicken from the pot and fry it lightly in hot vegetable oil until the outside becomes golden brown. If you prefer, you can grill or air-fry the chicken instead. Set it aside.

Wash the tomatoes and tatashe thoroughly. Blend them together until smooth. Pour the blended mixture into a pot and boil for about 10 to 15 minutes to reduce the excess water and remove the raw taste.
Heat the vegetable oil in a clean pot. Add the remaining chopped onion and sauté for about 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant and slightly translucent.

Pour the reduced tomato mixture into the hot oil and fry over medium heat for about 15 to 20 minutes, stirring regularly to prevent burning. Continue frying until the stew thickens and the oil begins to separate from the tomato mixture.
Pour in a little of the reserved chicken stock to achieve your preferred consistency. Taste and adjust the seasoning by adding more salt or seasoning cubes if necessary.

Return the fried chicken to the stew and gently stir to coat every piece with the rich tomato sauce. Allow everything to simmer together for another 8 to 10 minutes so the chicken absorbs the flavor of the stew.
Remove from the heat and serve hot with white rice, boiled yam, boiled potatoes, fried plantain, bread, pasta, or any side dish of your choice.

name: Ofada Rice and Ayamase Stew
description: A bold and distinctive Nigerian dish featuring locally grown Ofada rice served with rich Ayamase (designer) stew. The stew is made with green tatashe, scotch bonnet peppers, bleached palm oil, iru (locust beans), and assorted meat, creating the signature spicy and smoky flavour that makes this Yoruba delicacy a favourite at parties and special occasions.
instructions: Pick through the Ofada rice carefully to remove stones, husks, or other debris. Wash it thoroughly in several changes of clean water until the water runs fairly clear. Transfer the rice to a pot, add enough water to cover it, and cook over medium heat for 30–35 minutes or until the grains are soft but not mushy. Drain any excess water if necessary and keep the rice warm.
Wash the green tatashe and scotch bonnet peppers thoroughly. Remove the stalks, roughly chop them, and blend into a coarse paste with very little or no water. Set the pepper mixture aside.

Wash the assorted meat and place it in a pot. Add seasoning cubes, a little salt, and enough water to cook the meat. Simmer until the meat becomes tender, then reserve both the cooked meat and the stock.

Pour the palm oil into a clean pot and bleach it over medium heat until it changes from bright red to a light brown colour. Reduce the heat immediately once it reaches this stage to avoid burning the oil.
Add the iru (locust beans) to the bleached palm oil and fry gently for about 2 minutes while stirring continuously. This helps release the distinctive aroma that gives Ayamase its signature flavour.

Pour the blended green pepper mixture into the pot and fry over medium heat for 15–20 minutes. Stir occasionally to prevent burning until the moisture evaporates and the oil begins to separate and float on top of the stew.

Add the cooked assorted meat together with a small quantity of the reserved meat stock. Stir well so the meat is fully coated with the sauce. Taste and adjust the seasoning by adding more salt or seasoning cubes if needed.
Allow the stew to simmer gently for another 10–15 minutes so the flavours combine properly and the sauce thickens to a rich consistency.
Serve the hot Ayamase stew generously over the cooked Ofada rice. For an authentic presentation, wrap the rice in banana leaves before serving if available.

name: Coconut Rice
description: Fragrant and creamy Nigerian coconut rice cooked in rich coconut milk with tender chicken, peppers, and aromatic seasonings. This delicious one-pot meal has a rich coconut flavour that pairs perfectly with fried plantain or salad and is ideal for everyday meals or special occasions.
instructions: Wash the rice thoroughly in clean water until the water runs almost clear. Drain and set aside. If using parboiled rice, partially cook it for about 8–10 minutes, drain, and set aside.

Wash the chicken thoroughly and season with salt, seasoning cubes, onions (optional), curry, and thyme. Cook until tender, then lightly fry the chicken in vegetable oil until golden brown. Set the chicken aside and reserve the stock.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onions and sauté for 2–3 minutes until soft and fragrant without allowing them to brown.
Add the washed rice to the pot and stir gently for about 2 minutes so the grains become lightly coated with the oil and onions.
Pour in the coconut milk and add enough reserved chicken stock or water to cook the rice. Stir well to combine all the ingredients.
Add the cooked chicken, whole or sliced scotch bonnet peppers, seasoning cubes, and salt to taste. Stir gently to distribute everything evenly.
Cover the pot tightly and cook over low heat for 20–25 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent the rice from sticking to the bottom. Add a little more hot water only if necessary.

When the rice is tender and all the liquid has been absorbed, remove the peppers if you prefer a milder flavour, fluff the rice gently with a fork, and allow it to rest for about 5 minutes before serving.
Serve the coconut rice hot with fried plantain, steamed vegetables, salad, or your favourite chilled drink.

name: Nigerian Beans Porridge
description: A comforting and nutritious Nigerian one-pot meal made with soft-cooked brown beans, ripe plantain, palm oil, crayfish, and aromatic seasonings. Rich in protein, fibre, and essential nutrients, this hearty dish is satisfying enough to be enjoyed on its own or with a chilled drink.
instructions: Pick through the brown beans to remove stones, damaged beans, or dirt. Rinse thoroughly under clean running water. If you want to reduce the cooking time, soak the beans in clean water for about 30 minutes before cooking, then drain.

Transfer the beans into a large pot and add enough water to cover them completely. Place the pot over medium heat and cook for about 35–40 minutes, adding more hot water whenever necessary until the beans begin to soften.
While the beans are cooking, peel the ripe plantains and cut them into medium-sized chunks. Set them aside until the beans are partially cooked.
Add the chopped onion, palm oil, crayfish, seasoning cubes, and salt to the pot. Stir thoroughly until the palm oil dissolves into the beans and everything is well combined.
Add the chopped plantain pieces to the pot. Stir gently so the plantain is evenly distributed, then cover the pot and continue cooking over low to medium heat.

Cook for another 15–20 minutes until both the beans and plantain become very soft. Stir occasionally to prevent the porridge from sticking to the bottom of the pot. Add a little hot water if the porridge becomes too thick before the beans are fully cooked.
Taste the porridge and adjust the seasoning if needed. If you prefer a creamier consistency, use the back of a spoon to mash some of the cooked beans while leaving some whole beans for texture.
Allow the beans porridge to simmer for another 3–5 minutes so all the flavours blend together perfectly. Remove from the heat and allow it to rest for a few minutes before serving.
Serve the beans porridge hot on its own or with fried fish, boiled eggs, fried plantain, or a chilled drink for a complete and satisfying Nigerian meal.

name: Yam and Egg Sauce
description: A simple and beloved Nigerian breakfast of boiled yam served with a spicy tomato and egg sauce. Quick to prepare and deeply satisfying, it is a staple meal enjoyed in many Nigerian homes for breakfast, lunch, or dinner.
instructions: Peel the yam and cut it into medium-sized slices. Rinse thoroughly to remove excess starch.
Place the yam in a pot, add enough water to cover it, season lightly with salt if desired, and boil for 20–25 minutes until tender. Drain and set aside.
Dice the tomatoes, onions, and fresh pepper if using. Beat the eggs in a bowl and season lightly with a pinch of salt and black pepper.
Heat the vegetable oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Add the onions and sauté for about 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and pepper, then cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally until the tomatoes soften and the excess moisture reduces.
Pour the beaten eggs into the tomato mixture. Stir gently and continuously until the eggs are cooked but still soft and moist.
Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. Serve the hot egg sauce alongside the boiled yam.

name: Bole and Fish
description: A popular Nigerian street food from Rivers State — roasted unripe plantain served with grilled fish and a spicy pepper sauce. Smoky, satisfying, and completely irresistible.
instructions: Peel plantain and brush lightly with oil.
Roast plantain over open flame or grill until charred.
Season fish with salt, pepper, and spices.
Grill fish until cooked through.
Blend peppers and onion; fry briefly in oil.
Serve roasted plantain with grilled fish and pepper sauce.

name: Plantain and Egg Stir Fry
description: A quick and delicious Nigerian breakfast that combines sweet fried ripe plantain with fluffy scrambled eggs, peppers, and onions. Ready in under 30 minutes, this satisfying meal delivers a perfect balance of sweetness, protein, and flavor for breakfast, brunch, or a light dinner.
instructions: Peel the ripe plantains and slice them into medium-thick diagonal or round pieces.
Heat the vegetable oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Fry the plantain slices for 2–3 minutes on each side until golden brown. Remove and drain on paper towels.
Dice the onion and green pepper into small pieces. Beat the eggs in a bowl and season lightly with salt and black pepper.
Remove excess oil from the pan, leaving about one tablespoon. Add the onions and green pepper, then sauté for 2–3 minutes until softened and fragrant.
Pour the beaten eggs into the pan and stir gently with a spatula until they begin to set into soft scrambled eggs.
Add the fried plantain back into the pan and gently fold everything together without breaking the plantain pieces.
Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. Serve immediately while hot, with a chilled drink or fresh fruit if desired.

name: Yam Pottage (Asaro)
description: A creamy and comforting Nigerian yam pottage cooked in a rich tomato and palm oil sauce with onions, crayfish, and spices until the yam becomes soft and slightly mashed. This classic one-pot meal is hearty, flavorful, and perfect for lunch or dinner.
instructions: Peel the yam and cut it into medium-sized cubes. Rinse thoroughly under clean water to remove excess starch.
Blend or finely chop the tomatoes, onion, and fresh pepper if using. Set aside.
Place the yam in a pot, add enough water to cover it slightly, then add half of the chopped onion and cook over medium heat for about 10 minutes until the yam is partially cooked.
Add the blended tomato mixture, palm oil, crayfish, seasoning cubes, salt, and any preferred spices. Stir gently to combine without breaking the yam.
Cover the pot and continue cooking for another 15–20 minutes until the yam becomes very soft and absorbs the rich sauce.
Lightly mash a few pieces of the yam with the back of a spoon to naturally thicken the pottage while leaving most of the cubes intact.
Taste and adjust the seasoning if necessary. Serve hot on its own or with smoked fish, boiled eggs, or vegetables.

name: Indomie Stir Fry
description: A Nigerian staple—spiced instant noodles stir-fried with eggs, vegetables, and sausage for a quick, filling, and delicious family meal. Perfect for busy days and ready in under 30 minutes.
instructions: Boil the noodles for 2–3 minutes; drain and set aside.
Heat vegetable oil in a large pan and fry the sliced sausage until lightly browned.
Add the mixed vegetables and stir-fry for 2–3 minutes.
Push the vegetables to one side of the pan and scramble the eggs.
Add the cooked noodles and seasoning sachets.
Stir everything together until evenly combined.
Serve hot.

name: Kilishi
description: A Northern Nigerian delicacy of thin spiced dried beef marinated in a rich groundnut and spice paste, then sun-dried or oven-dried to perfection. A protein-packed snack with bold, complex flavors.
instructions: Slice the beef very thinly against the grain.
Mix the groundnut paste with suya spice, ginger powder, garlic powder, and a little water to form a smooth paste.
Coat the beef slices evenly with the spice mixture.
Arrange the slices on a drying rack and sun-dry for 6–8 hours, or oven-dry at 70°C.
Halfway through drying, flip the slices and lightly re-coat with the spice mixture if desired.
Continue drying until the beef becomes firm and leathery.
Allow to cool completely before serving or storing in an airtight container.

name: Gizdodo
description: A popular Nigerian party appetizer combining tender seasoned chicken gizzard with sweet fried ripe plantain in a spicy pepper sauce. A perfect balance of savory and sweet in every bite.
instructions: Season and cook the gizzard until tender.
Heat oil and fry the cooked gizzard until slightly crispy; set aside.
Slice the ripe plantain and fry until golden brown; set aside.
Blend the tatashe with pepper and fry in the remaining oil for about 10 minutes.
Add the fried gizzard and plantain to the sauce.
Toss gently and cook for another 5 minutes.
Serve hot as an appetizer, side dish, or party snack.

name: Nigerian Spring Rolls
description: Crispy golden Nigerian-style spring rolls filled with a spiced minced meat and vegetable filling, deep fried to perfection. A crowd-pleasing party snack that disappears fast.
instructions: Fry minced meat with onion and spices until cooked.
Add vegetables and stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Allow the filling to cool completely.
Place filling on each pastry sheet and roll tightly.
Seal the edges with a flour-and-water paste.
Deep fry in hot oil until golden brown and crispy.
Drain on paper towels and serve with pepper sauce.

name: Puff Puff
description: A beloved Nigerian deep-fried dough snack that is soft, fluffy, and slightly sweet inside with a golden crispy exterior. A staple at every Nigerian party and gathering.
instructions: Mix flour, sugar, yeast, and a pinch of salt in a large bowl.
Gradually add warm water while mixing until you have a smooth, thick batter.
Cover the bowl and allow the batter to rise for 45–60 minutes or until doubled in size.
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep pot over medium heat.
Scoop small portions of batter into the hot oil using a spoon or your hand.
Fry until the puff puffs are golden brown on all sides, turning occasionally.
Drain on paper towels and serve warm.

name: Okpa

name: Seafood Okra Rice

name: Tomato Rice with Chicken

author: API Food Database

name: Nigerian Omelette and Bread

author: API Food Database

name: Masa with Miyan Taushe

author: API Food Database

name: Nigerian Pepper Chicken
description: Tender chicken pieces cooked in a bold and fiery Nigerian pepper sauce made from blended scotch bonnet, tatashe, and onions. A spicy and aromatic dish that pairs perfectly with rice, yam, or bread.

name: Okra Soup
description: A thick and hearty Nigerian okra soup made with freshly sliced okra, palm oil, assorted meats, and seafood. The natural drawing quality of okra creates a uniquely satisfying texture loved across all Nigerian tribes.

author: API Food Database

name: Groundnut Soup
description: A rich and creamy Northern Nigerian soup made from roasted groundnut paste simmered with chicken, tomatoes, and aromatic spices. Nutty, hearty, and deeply satisfying—best served with tuwo shinkafa, rice, or fufu.

name: Fisherman Soup

name: Abak Atama Soup

Add meat and seasoning; stir well.

author: API Food Database

name: Nigerian Fried Rice with Shrimp

name: Amala and Ewedu

name: Semovita and Okra Soup

Cook okra soup with palm oil, meat, and crayfish.

Serve semovita alongside okra soup.
author: API Food Database

author: API Food Database

name: Peppered Turkey
description: A festive Nigerian party staple of fried turkey pieces coated in a rich and spicy pepper stew. Deeply flavored, tender on the inside, and crispy on the outside—a must-have at every Nigerian celebration.
instructions: Wash and season the turkey pieces with salt, seasoning cubes, thyme, curry, garlic, and ginger.
Cook until tender, reserving the stock.
Deep fry or air fry the turkey until golden brown and slightly crispy.
Blend the tatashe, scotch bonnet, and onion until smooth.
Heat vegetable oil in a pan and fry the blended pepper mixture for about 20 minutes until the oil separates.
Season the pepper sauce to taste and add a little reserved turkey stock if needed.
Add the fried turkey pieces and toss until evenly coated.
Simmer for 8–10 minutes so the turkey absorbs the pepper sauce.
Serve hot as a party appetizer or with fried rice, jollof rice, or chips.
